QF.id: AIFM CII Fund Monitoring Reporting and Exit_25

question.text: Under what circumstances does Chapter 12 describe a promoter buyback (via put option) as appropriate?

answer.text: As the default first-choice exit, superior to IPO because of price certainty.
As a mandatory exit in every portfolio company from year 3 of investment.
Only in listed-company contexts where promoter resources are automatically adequate.
As a residual / last-resort exit in a going-concern context, usually after IPO and other exits are not available.

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 12: 'Put prices guarantee a certain return or IRR ... The promoters may stipulate that the "put" shall be a residual option not exercisable unless the company does not go public within an agreed time frame or the AIF could not avail of other exit mechanisms stated above. These are the reasons why a buyback option may not be a feasible option in every case. It is usually used as a last resort in a going concern context.' The Trap: Default first-choice (Option A) reverses the Chapter's clear hierarchy. Mandatory year-3 buyback (Option B) is invented. Listed-company framing (Option C) is wrong — buyback works BETTER in unlisted contexts per Chapter 12. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C identical framing. Put-option structuring is a Cat I/II negotiation skill, not a Cat III topic. Manager's Pro-Tip: Draft the put formula explicitly in the shareholders' agreement — a typical Indian VC put is 'invested amount compounded at 18% IRR or 2.5x, whichever is higher.' Vague put formulas cause litigation when exercised.
